periods.activity_title: Place Value Unpacked: Reading Decimals Aloud

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 1, section 12.2 p.69

time_bands.activity: Students read 27.53 aloud and break it into place-value parts — 2 tens, 7 units, 5 tenths, 3 hundredths — on a chart drawn in their notebooks, internalising how the decimal point separates whole parts from fractional parts.

Using the spice-buying context from section 12.1, students express 50 g, 100 g, 25 g, and 250 g as fractions of 1 kg, then rewrite each as a decimal, discovering that denominators of 10, 100, and 1000 map directly to tenths, hundredths, and thousandths columns.

A class-wide fraction–decimal game (mirroring the Jonali–Pallabi game in section 12.1): teacher calls a fraction, pairs race to write the decimal and say the place-value reading aloud, reinforcing the connection between denominator size and decimal depth.

Students derive the divide-by-power-of-ten rule from the pattern 123 ÷ 10 = 12.3, 24 ÷ 100 = 0.24, 12 ÷ 1000 = 0.012, then practise Example 1, section 12.2 p.69 ("Arshad buys 5 pens at ₹9.5 each….") as a preview of how this rule carries into multiplication.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who place the decimal point one position off when dividing by 10 — a common slip when the dividend has no existing decimal point. Use 123 ÷ 10 = 12.3 and 24 ÷ 100 = 0.24 side by side to show that counting zeroes in the divisor tells exactly how many places to shift.

periods.activity_title: Shifting the Point: Powers of Ten in Practice

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 12.2 p.73–74
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete a table multiplying 5.7, 23.02, 0.92, 0.306, and 24.67 by 10, 100, and 1000.

time_bands.activity: Quick mental drill: teacher writes 5 division expressions (e.g., 456 ÷ 100, 7 ÷ 1000) on the board; students write answers on slates, applying the shift-left rule established through the place-value pattern from section 12.1.

Students work Figure it Out Q10, section 12.2 p.73–74 ("Complete a table multiplying 5.7, 23.02, 0.92, 0.306, and 24.67 by 10, 100, and 1000.") individually, then compare in pairs — noticing the symmetry between multiplying (shift right) and dividing (shift left) by powers of ten.

Class discussion: students identify which of the numbers in the table are greater than 1 before and after multiplying by 10, 100, 1000, building an early intuition about how the decimal point's position determines size — a foundation for the sign-of-size reasoning in section 12.2.
Brief oral summary: each student states one thing the decimal point's movement tells them about a number's size; teacher collects misconceptions for the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse the direction of the shift when moving between multiplication and division by powers of ten — reinforce the mnemonic 'multiplication moves right, division moves left' with colour-coded arrows on the board. The table in Figure it Out Q10 makes the symmetric pattern visible across many numbers at once, which helps consolidate it.

periods.activity_title: Fraction Bridges: Multiplying Decimals Through Fractions

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 1, section 12.2 p.69
Example 2, section 12.2 p.69
textbook_items_in_class.description: A car travels 12.5 km per litre; distance on 7.5 litres = 12.5 × 7.5 = (125×75)/(10×10) = 9375/100 = 93.75 km.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 3, section 12.2 p.70
textbook_items_in_class.description: Ajay walks 827 m (0.827 km) each way to school, twice a day, 6 days a week: 0.827 × 2 = 1.654 km/day, and 1.654 × 6 = 9.924 km/week.

time_bands.activity: Teacher walks through Example 1, section 12.2 p.69 ("Arshad buys 5 pens at ₹9.5 each….") on the board, converting 9.5 to 95/10, multiplying, and reading off the decimal answer — students see the fraction route as a bridge to the decimal product.

Students work Example 2, section 12.2 p.69 ("A car travels 12.5 km per litre; distance on 7.5 litres….") in pairs, converting both decimals to fractions, multiplying numerators, combining denominators, and converting back — teacher circulates to check denominator handling.

Students attempt Example 3, section 12.2 p.70 ("Ajay walks 827 m (0.827 km) each way to school, twice a day, 6 days….") individually; with three decimal places in 0.827, they must track the denominator 1000 through two multiplications, noticing how the number of decimal places accumulates.

Class pools the three results into a small table showing decimal places in each factor and in the product, prompting students to conjecture aloud what pattern they see before the rule is formalised in section 12.2.

periods.teacher_notes: The most persistent error here is mishandling the denominator when both factors are decimals — students often use 10 instead of 100 for a product of two one-decimal-place numbers. Keep Example 2 on the board alongside Example 1 so students can see that each factor's denominator contributes independently. Example 4, section 12.2 p.70 ("Area of a rectangle with sides 5.7 cm and 13.3 cm….") offers a self-study extension for those who finish early.

periods.activity_title: Count the Places: The Decimal Multiplication Rule

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 5, section 12.2 p.72
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 5.8 × 1.24 using the rule: 58 × 124 = 7192, and with 1 + 2 = 3 decimal places the product is 7.192.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.2 p.73
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the products in tenths, hundredths, etc.: (a) 6 × 4 tenths; (b) 7 × 0.3; (c) 9 × 5 hundredths.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 12.2 p.73
Figure it Out Q8, section 12.2 p.73

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 12.2 p.73
homework.description: Thejus needs 1.65 m of cloth for a shirt; find the cloth needed for 3 shirts.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates Example 5, section 12.2 p.72 ("Find 5.8 × 1.24 using the rule: 58 × 124 = 7192….") live: strip the points, multiply whole numbers, then restore the point by counting total decimal places — students copy and verify by the fraction route.

Students solve Figure it Out Q1, section 12.2 p.73 ("Find the products in tenths, hundredths, etc….") and Figure it Out Q2, section 12.2 p.73 ("Find the products (a) 27.34 × 6; (b) 4.23 × 3.7; (c) 0.432 × 0.23.") applying the count-the-places rule independently.

Students work Figure it Out Q8, section 12.2 p.73 ("Given 18 × 12 = 216, find (a) 18 × 1.2; (b) 18 × 0.12….") — a chain of multiplications from the same whole-number fact — consolidating how point placement shifts as decimal places are added and identifying which products fall below 1.

Class compiles a three-row summary on the board: both factors > 1, both between 0 and 1, one of each — students predict and then confirm the size of the product in each row, preparing them for the sign-of-size questions in Figure it Out Q9.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent slip when applying the count-the-places rule is inserting the decimal point one place too far left in the product — particularly when the stripped multiplication itself ends in a zero. Figure it Out Q8 is ideal for catching this because each step in the chain uses the same whole-number product 216. Figure it Out Q3, section 12.2 p.73 ("Thejus needs 1.65 m of cloth for a shirt….") is set for home reinforcement.

periods.activity_title: Bigger or Smaller? Reasoning About Products

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 12.2 p.73
textbook_items_in_class.description: Without multiplying, decide which products are less than 1: (a) 7 × 0.6; (b) 0.7 × 0.6; (c) 0.7 × 6; (d) 0.07 × 0.06.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 12.2 p.73
textbook_items_in_class.description: Meenu buys 4 notebooks at ₹15.50 and 3 erasers at ₹2.75 each; find the total spent.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 12.2 p.73
textbook_items_in_class.description: A rupee coin is 1.45 mm thick; find the total height in centimetres of a stack of 36 coins.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 12.2 p.73
textbook_items_in_class.description: Oranges cost ₹56.50 per kg; find the price of 2.250 kg, and decide whether writing 56.50 as 56.5 and 2.250 as 2.25 gives the same product and why.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 12.2 p.73
textbook_items_in_class.description: Dwarakanath buys notebooks at ₹23.6 wholesale and sells at ₹30 each; find the profit on selling 50 books in a week.

time_bands.activity: Students attempt Figure it Out Q9, section 12.2 p.73 ("Without multiplying, decide which products are less than 1….") using only reasoning about factor sizes — they must articulate why, not just state which — building the habit of justification from the three-category framework developed in the previous unit.

Students work Figure it Out Q4, section 12.2 p.73 ("Meenu buys 4 notebooks at ₹15.50 and 3 erasers at ₹2.75 each…."), Figure it Out Q5, section 12.2 p.73 ("A rupee coin is 1.45 mm thick; find the total height…."), and Figure it Out Q7, section 12.2 p.73 ("Dwarakanath buys notebooks at ₹23.6 wholesale….") in small groups, applying decimal multiplication to real-world totals and profit.

Class discusses Figure it Out Q6, section 12.2 p.73 ("Oranges cost ₹56.50 per kg; find the price of 2.250 kg, and decide whether writing 56.50 as 56.5….") — students reason why trailing zeroes after the last significant digit do not change the decimal's value, grounding their argument in place value rather than a rule.
Brief exit reflection: each student writes one sentence explaining in their own words why a product of two numbers both less than 1 must itself be less than 1.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes assert that 'multiplying always makes a number bigger' — the three-category table from section 12.2 directly confronts this. Encourage students to test their Q9 reasoning against actual computation for at least one example, building the verification habit the NCF emphasises. Figure it Out Q5 often trips students who forget to convert mm to cm after multiplying.

periods.activity_title: Dividing by Powers of Ten and Equivalent Fractions

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 6, section 12.3 p.74
textbook_items_in_class.description: Anuja cuts a 3.9 m ribbon into 10 equal pieces: 3.9 ÷ 10 = (39/10) × (1/10) = 39/100 = 0.39 m each (and into 100 pieces gives 0.039 m).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 7, section 12.3 p.75–76
Figure it Out Q1, section 12.3 p.83
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the quotient by converting the denominator into 1, 10, 100, or 1000 and verify by long division: (a) 18/5; (b) 415/4; (c) 1217/2; (d) 4827/8.

time_bands.activity: Teacher works Example 6, section 12.3 p.74 ("Anuja cuts a 3.9 m ribbon into 10 equal pieces….") on the board, showing that dividing a decimal by 10 is equivalent to multiplying its fractional form by 1/10 — the point shifts left exactly one place.

Students work Example 7, section 12.3 p.75–76 ("29 m of ribbon shared by 2….") in pairs, first trying the equivalent-fraction method for ÷ 2 and ÷ 4, then verifying that denominators 2 and 4 both have equivalents over powers of ten.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q1, section 12.3 p.83 ("Find the quotient by converting the denominator into 1, 10, 100, or 1000….") individually — the four parts span denominators 2, 4, 5, and 8, testing whether each can be scaled to a power of ten.

Class compiles results: students identify which denominators (2, 4, 5, 8) yield whole powers of ten and conjecture which divisors will always give terminating decimals — a question section 12.4 will answer formally.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often forget to adjust the numerator when scaling the denominator to a power of ten — for example, scaling 4 to 100 requires multiplying both numerator and denominator by 25. The verification step in Figure it Out Q1 (long division) is worth insisting on so students build confidence that both methods yield identical quotients.

periods.activity_title: Long Division Extended: Decimal Quotients Step by Step

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 8, section 12.3 p.77
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 1324 ÷ 4 by division using place value (long division), regrouping thousands into hundreds, etc.: 1324 ÷ 4 = 331.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 9, section 12.3 p.81
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 237 ÷ 8 by long division with a decimal quotient, regrouping ones into tenths, tenths into hundredths, hundredths into thousandths: 237 ÷ 8 = 29.625.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 10, section 12.3 p.82
textbook_items_in_class.description: A shopkeeper packs 9.5 kg of sugar equally into 4 bags: 9.5 ÷ 4 = 2.375 kg per bag, placing the decimal point before dividing the tenths.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 12.3 p.83
Figure it Out Q4, section 12.3 p.83

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates Example 8, section 12.3 p.77 ("Find 1324 ÷ 4 by division using place value….") as a warm-up — regrouping thousands into hundreds, hundreds into tens, and so on — refreshing the place-value division procedure before the decimal point enters.

Teacher works Example 9, section 12.3 p.81 ("Find 237 ÷ 8 by long division with a decimal quotient….") step by step, pausing when ones are first regrouped into tenths and explicitly placing the decimal point in the quotient at that moment — students annotate their own written work.

Students try Example 10, section 12.3 p.82 ("A shopkeeper packs 9.5 kg of sugar equally into 4 bags….") independently — the dividend already has a decimal, so they must recognise when to place the point in the quotient from the very first step.

Students begin Figure it Out Q3, section 12.3 p.83 ("Find the quotient (a) 132 ÷ 4; (b) 13.2 ÷ 4; (c) 1.32 ÷ 4; (d) 0.132 ÷ 4.") and Figure it Out Q4, section 12.3 p.83 ("Find the quotient (a) 126 ÷ 8; (b) 12.6 ÷ 8….") in pairs — the chain structure shows how shifting the decimal point in the dividend shifts it in the quotient.

periods.teacher_notes: The critical moment students miss is exactly when to write the decimal point in the quotient — it goes in as soon as the ones digit has been divided and the remainder is regrouped into tenths. Example 10 is particularly diagnostic because the dividend itself begins with a decimal. Figure it Out Q4 spans five levels of the same division, making patterns in the quotient very visible.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 11, section 12.3 p.83
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 0.06 ÷ 5 by place value: 0 ones, 0 tenths, 6 hundredths give 1 hundredth with remainder regrouped into thousandths, so 0.06 ÷ 5 = 0.012.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 12, section 12.3 p.84
textbook_items_in_class.description: Ravi covers 126 km in 2.5 hours; average speed = 126 ÷ 2.5. Converting the divisor: 126 × (10/25) = 1260/25 = 50.4 km/h.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 13, section 12.3 p.84
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 4.68 ÷ 1.3 and 4.68 ÷ 0.13 by making the divisor a whole number: multiply dividend and divisor by the same power of ten, so 4.68 ÷ 0.13 = 468 ÷ 13.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 12.3 p.86
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the quotients (a) 24.86 ÷ 1.2; (b) 5.728 ÷ 1.52.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 12.3 p.87
textbook_items_in_class.description: A 4 m wooden block is cut into 5 equal pieces; find the length of each piece.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 12.3 p.87
textbook_items_in_class.description: A regular 12-sided polygon has perimeter 208.8 cm; find the length of its side.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 12.3 p.87
textbook_items_in_class.description: 3 litres of watermelon juice is shared equally among 8 friends; find each share in millilitres.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 12.3 p.87
homework.description: A car covers 234.45 km using 12.6 litres of petrol; find the distance travelled per litre.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates Example 11, section 12.3 p.83 ("Find 0.06 ÷ 5 by place value….") and Example 12, section 12.3 p.84 ("Ravi covers 126 km in 2.5 hours; average speed = 126 ÷ 2.5….") back to back, contrasting dividing a small decimal by a whole number with dividing a whole number by a decimal divisor.

Teacher demonstrates Example 13, section 12.3 p.84 ("Find 4.68 ÷ 1.3 and 4.68 ÷ 0.13 by making the divisor a whole number….") — students articulate the rule: multiply both dividend and divisor by the same power of ten so the divisor becomes a whole number, then divide as usual.

Students solve Figure it Out Q2, section 12.3 p.86 ("Find the quotients (a) 24.86 ÷ 1.2; (b) 5.728 ÷ 1.52.") and three word problems — Figure it Out Q6, section 12.3 p.87 ("A 4 m wooden block is cut into 5 equal pieces…."), Figure it Out Q7, section 12.3 p.87 ("A regular 12-sided polygon has perimeter 208.8 cm…."), and Figure it Out Q8, section 12.3 p.87 ("3 litres of watermelon juice is shared equally among 8 friends….") — in small groups.
Groups share one word-problem solution each; class evaluates whether the decimal point in the quotient is correctly placed, with particular attention to problems where the divisor is a decimal.

periods.teacher_notes: When dividing by a decimal divisor, students commonly multiply only the dividend by the power of ten and leave the divisor unchanged — stress that both must be multiplied by the same value to preserve the quotient. Figure it Out Q9, section 12.3 p.87 ("A car covers 234.45 km using 12.6 litres….") is set for home reinforcement, as it combines a decimal divisor with a context identical to Example 12.

periods.activity_title: When Does Division Ever End? Cycles and Conjectures

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.3 p.86
textbook_items_in_class.description: Express in decimal form: (a) 2/5; (b) 13/4; (c) 4/50; (d) 5/8.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 12.3 p.86–87
Figure it Out Q4, section 12.3 p.87
Figure it Out Q5, section 12.3 p.87
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the quotient (a) 2.46 ÷ 1.5; (b) 2.46 ÷ 0.15; (c) 2.46 ÷ 0.015, and decide whether 24.6 ÷ 1.5 equals 2.46 ÷ 0.15.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 12.3 p.87
homework.description: 13.5 kg of flour is distributed equally among 15 students; find each student's share.

time_bands.activity: Students divide 10 ÷ 3 by long division, recording each step and remainder, until they notice the remainder 1 keeps recurring — teacher asks: 'Will this ever end?' Students articulate why it cannot: the remainder cycles, so the quotient 3.333… never terminates.

Students compute 1 ÷ 7, again recording remainders and quotient digits through at least six steps, discovering the repeating block 142857 — teacher introduces the 'magic number' and its cyclic property (multiplying by 1–6 gives permutations of the same digits), connecting to Emil Artin's unsolved 1927 conjecture noted in section 12.3.

Students work Figure it Out Q4, section 12.3 p.87 ("Evaluate (a) 25 ÷ __ = 0.025; (b) 25 ÷ __ = 250….") and Figure it Out Q5, section 12.3 p.87 ("Find the quotient (a) 2.46 ÷ 1.5; (b) 2.46 ÷ 0.15; (c) 2.46 ÷ 0.015….") in pairs, consolidating the dividend–divisor–quotient relationship; Figure it Out Q1, section 12.3 p.86 ("Express in decimal form: (a) 2/5; (b) 13/4; (c) 4/50; (d) 5/8.") and Figure it Out Q3, section 12.3 p.86–87 ("Using 156 × 12 = 1872, evaluate….") also available for fast finishers.

Open discussion: students conjecture which fractions 1/n produce repeating decimals and which terminate, based on what they have seen — the class keeps a tally on the board of divisors tested so far, preparing the question that section 12.4 answers.

periods.teacher_notes: Students are often intrigued and then confused by non-terminating decimals — use the long-division remainder trace to show concretely why 10 ÷ 3 cannot terminate: a remainder of 1 always produces another 3 in the quotient, and so on without end. The magic-number exploration of 142857 is a high-engagement moment; Figure it Out Q10, section 12.3 p.87 is set for home practice.

periods.activity_title: Leap Years by Decimal: Accumulating the Extra Hours

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: A 210 g packet of peanut chikki costs ₹70.5 and a 110 g packet of potato chips costs ₹33.25; decide which is cheaper (per gram).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 12.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Shyamala buys 3 kg of bananas at ₹30/kg, counts 35 bananas, and sells each at ₹5; find her profit on selling all.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 12.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Textbooks 2.5 cm thick are placed on a 160 cm shelf; find how many of 80 books fit and whether any space is left.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 12.4 p.94
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill the blanks using the given conversions: 5.5 km = __ m; 35 cm = __ m; 14.5 cm = __ mm; 68 g = __ kg; 9.02 m = __ mm; 125.5 ml = __ l.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the leap-year problem from section 12.4: the Earth takes 365.2422 days per orbit, so students calculate 0.2422 × 100 = 24.22 extra days per century, motivating why adding a day every four years is an approximation that still needs correction.

Students build the divisibility decision chart from section 12.4 — divisible by 4? by 100? by 400? — and compute (24 × 366) + (76 × 365) for a century, then compare with 100 × 365.2422 = 36,524.22, expressing and evaluating each step as a decimal multiplication.

Students work Figure it Out Q1, section 12.4 p.93 ("A 210 g packet of peanut chikki costs ₹70.5…."), Figure it Out Q3, section 12.4 p.93 ("Shyamala buys 3 kg of bananas…."), Figure it Out Q4, section 12.4 p.93 ("Textbooks 2.5 cm thick are placed on a 160 cm shelf…."), and Figure it Out Q5, section 12.4 p.94 ("Fill the blanks using the given conversions….") in small groups, applying decimal multiplication and division in measurement and commercial contexts.
Brief group share: one group explains the shelf-packing answer, another the per-gram price comparison — class checks that unit conversions were handled before the division, not after.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often forget to divide by the weight (in grams) when computing per-gram price, treating it as a per-kg problem — Figure it Out Q1 is a good diagnostic for this. The leap-year calculation connects decimal multiplication to a real astronomical context, but students need to see the full four-term millennium sum explicitly to understand why the every-4, skip-100, keep-400 rule is progressively more accurate.

periods.activity_title: Why Do Some Decimals Terminate? Denominators of 2s and 5s

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 12.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write the decimal number at each arrow mark on the given number lines (between 3.1 and 3.2, and between 2.15 and 2.17).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 12.4 p.94
textbook_items_in_class.description: Sridharacharya's Patiganita problem: 6¼ divided by 2½ and 60¼ divided by 3½; solve by converting the fractions into decimals.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 12.4 p.94
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill the boxes in at least 2 different ways: (a) __ × __ = 2.4; (b) __ × __ = 14.5.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 12.4 p.94
Figure it Out Q9, section 12.4 p.94
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill in the missing cells of a table where each cell represents a ÷ b, given values 1517, 151.7, 15.17, 1.517, 15170 and divisors 37, 3.7, 0.37.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the table of 1/2, 1/(2×2), 1/(2×2×2),… and 1/5, 1/(5×5),… from section 12.4: students compute each decimal, observe that all terminate, and reason deductively — denominators built only from 2s and 5s can always be scaled to a power of ten, so the decimal must terminate.

Students work Figure it Out Q8, section 12.4 p.94 ("Given 756 ÷ 36 = 21, find (a) 75.6 ÷ 3.6; (b) 7.56 ÷ 0.36….") and Figure it Out Q9, section 12.4 p.94 ("Fill in the missing cells of a table where each cell represents a ÷ b…."), applying the multiplying-dividend-and-divisor-by-the-same-power rule at scale.

Students solve Figure it Out Q2, section 12.4 p.93 ("Write the decimal number at each arrow mark on the given number lines…."), Figure it Out Q6, section 12.4 p.94 ("Sridharacharya's Patiganita problem…."), and Figure it Out Q7, section 12.4 p.94 ("Fill the boxes in at least 2 different ways: (a) __ × __ = 2.4….") individually, covering number-line reading, historical problem-solving, and open multiplication tasks.

Class debrief: students share at least two different box-filling solutions for Figure it Out Q7, illustrating that decimal multiplication problems have multiple valid factor pairs — reinforcing creative and flexible thinking about decimals.

periods.teacher_notes: The core deductive argument — denominator factors of only 2s and 5s guarantee a power-of-ten equivalent — should be stated explicitly by at least one student before the teacher confirms it. Figure it Out Q9's table is a rich consolidation item because students must recognise that scaling both dividend and divisor preserves the quotient regardless of the decimal placement.

periods.activity_title: Decimals at Work: A Chapter Closing
periods.teacher_notes: Refer to Prepared Table (see material: 'Problems and solutions') for the problems in full and their worked solutions. Pose all three problems together on the board; students work individually in silence, showing every step. Then pairs compare working and reconstruct any disagreement step by step. One student per problem presents to the class; after each presentation the class names the chapter method used. Watch for: Problem 1 — students forgetting to count total decimal places (place-value rule for multiplication); Problem 2 — students misplacing the decimal point in the quotient, or regrouping the leftover tenths into tenths instead of hundredths (long division with a decimal dividend); Problem 3 — students trying to multiply the decimal divisor directly rather than first converting it to a whole number by multiplying both dividend and divisor by the same power of ten (decimal-divisor strategy). The closing band is the teacher's, not a student task.

visual_aids.title: Problems and solutions
visual_aids.table:
No. | Problem | Solution
1 | A rectangular plot measures 12.4 m by 8.75 m. What is its area in square metres? | Convert to fractions: 12.4 = 124/10, 8.75 = 875/100. Multiply whole numbers: 124 × 875 = 108500. Total decimal places: 1 + 2 = 3. Place point: 108.500 = 108.5 sq m.
2 | A water tank holds 46.8 litres. It is to be filled equally into 8 containers. How many litres does each container hold? | Divide 46.8 by 8 using long division. Units: 46 ÷ 8 = 5, remainder 6. Place the decimal point in the quotient now, before the tenths digit is written. Bring down the 8: 68 tenths ÷ 8 = 8 tenths, remainder 4 tenths. Regroup: 4 tenths = 40 hundredths, and 40 hundredths ÷ 8 = 5 hundredths. So 46.8 ÷ 8 = 5.85 litres each.
3 | A roll of ribbon 31.2 m long is cut into pieces each 0.48 m long. How many pieces are there? | Convert the decimal divisor: multiply both by 100, giving 3120 ÷ 48. Divide: 3120 ÷ 48 = 65. There are 65 pieces.

time_bands.activity: The three problems are written on the board and read aloud. Students are told to work each one individually, showing every step of the working — no calculators, no skipping.
Students work individually and in silence. The teacher circulates without correcting, noting which steps cause hesitation.
Students turn to their neighbour. Any pair with different answers reconstructs both solutions step by step to find where they diverge and agree on the correct route.

One student presents each problem at the board — full working, not just the answer. After each presentation the class names aloud the chapter method the solution rested on: decimal multiplication place-counting rule for Problem 1; long division extended to a decimal dividend for Problem 2; converting a decimal divisor to a whole number for Problem 3.

The teacher states the chapter's one idea: every operation on decimals — multiplication, division, whatever the context — is the same place-value arithmetic already known, with the decimal point placed by careful counting of places or by rescaling to remove it. That is why all three problems yielded.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly expresses the decimal 4.307 in expanded place-value form?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read each digit in its place-value column — ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths — in left-to-right order.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has shifted the place-value columns one position left, treating the digit before the decimal point as tens rather than ones.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has swapped the tenths and hundredths columns, placing 3 in the hundredths position instead of the tenths position.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has regrouped 3 tenths as 30 tenths, showing confusion between place value and digit face value.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to write the place-value table with column headings and place each digit of 4.307 into the correct column before choosing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write two more decimals in expanded form and then create a decimal from a given expanded form they write themselves.

items.prompt: Reena says the product 0.4 × 0.9 must be less than 0.4 because one of the factors is less than 1. Is she correct? Justify your answer using the behaviour of decimal products when both factors are between 0 and 1.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Reena is correct. When both factors are between 0 and 1, their product is less than either factor alone. Since 0.4 and 0.9 are both between 0 and 1, the product 0.4 × 0.9 = 0.36, which is indeed less than 0.4 (and less than 0.9).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the three-category sign-of-size rule from section 12.2: both factors between 0 and 1 gives a product smaller than either factor.

inclusivity.support: Let the student compute 0.4 × 0.9 by the fraction route (4/10 × 9/10 = 36/100) and compare 0.36 with 0.4 before writing the justification.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: what if one factor is between 0 and 1 and the other is greater than 1 — can the product be less than the factor that is greater than 1? Explain why.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 12.2 p.73
exercise.description: Without multiplying, decide which products are less than 1: (a) 7 × 0.6; (b) 0.7 × 0.6; (c) 0.7 × 6; (d) 0.07 × 0.06.

items.prompt: Explain why the decimal expansion of 1 ÷ 6 never ends. Use the long-division remainder trace to support your argument.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: When 1 is divided by 6 using long division, after the decimal point the remainders cycle: 10 ÷ 6 = 1 remainder 4; 40 ÷ 6 = 6 remainder 4; and the remainder 4 repeats indefinitely, so the digit 6 repeats forever and the decimal 0.1666… never terminates.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace the long-division remainders: once a remainder repeats, the corresponding quotient digits repeat, so the decimal cannot terminate.

inclusivity.support: Let the student carry out the long division of 1 ÷ 6 for at least five steps, writing the remainder at each step, before writing the explanation.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if 6 = 2 × 3, which of the prime factors 2 or 3 is responsible for the non-terminating decimal — and what would happen to the decimal if the denominator were 2 alone or 3 alone?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.3 p.86

items.prompt: The fraction 7/40 is said to give a terminating decimal. Using the fact that a fraction terminates when its denominator (in lowest terms) has only 2s and 5s as prime factors, explain whether this is true for 7/40.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 40 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5, so its only prime factors are 2 and 5. Since the denominator of 7/40 in lowest terms is 40, which has no prime factors other than 2 and 5, the decimal terminates. Multiplying numerator and denominator by 5 × 5 = 25 gives 175/1000 = 0.175, confirming termination.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Factorise the denominator and check for only 2s and 5s; then scale to a power of ten to verify the terminating decimal.

inclusivity.support: Let the student list the prime factors of 40 (using a factor tree) before applying the denominator rule.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find the smallest denominator greater than 40 that would make a fraction non-terminating, and explain why.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 12.4 p.93
exercise.description: Write the decimal number at each arrow mark on the given number lines (between 3.1 and 3.2, and between 2.15 and 2.17).

items.prompt: A spice shop sells turmeric in packets of 250 g. A customer buys 3 such packets. Express the total weight in kilograms as a decimal. Then, using the divide-by-power-of-ten rule, verify your answer by dividing the total weight in grams by 1000.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 packets × 250 g = 750 g. Dividing by 1000: write 750 with a decimal point as 750., count three zeroes, move the point three places left to get 0.750 = 0.75 kg. Both methods give 0.75 kg.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert grams to kilograms by dividing by 1000 using the shift-left rule established in section 12.1.

inclusivity.support: Let the student first place 750 on a place-value chart and physically move the decimal point left three positions, labelling each column.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to express the same weight in tonnes (1 tonne = 1 000 000 g) and explain how many places the decimal point must move.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 12.2 p.73–74
exercise.description: Complete a table multiplying 5.7, 23.02, 0.92, 0.306, and 24.67 by 10, 100, and 1000.

items.prompt: A ribbon is 3.6 m long. A craft shop needs 8.5 such ribbons for a display. Using the count-the-decimal-places rule, find the total length of ribbon needed in metres.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Strip the decimal points: 36 × 85 = 3060. Total decimal places: 1 (from 3.6) + 1 (from 8.5) = 2. Place the point two from the right: 30.60 = 30.6 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the whole numbers formed by stripping the decimal points, then restore the point by counting total decimal places in both factors.

inclusivity.support: Let the student convert 3.6 and 8.5 to fractions over powers of ten, multiply, and then read the decimal from the result before applying the rule.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to change 8.5 to 8.50 and verify that the extra trailing zero does not change the product, explaining why in terms of place value.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.2 p.73
exercise.description: Find the products in tenths, hundredths, etc.: (a) 6 × 4 tenths; (b) 7 × 0.3; (c) 9 × 5 hundredths.

items.prompt: A hardware shop sells wire at ₹18.4 per metre. A customer buys 12.5 m. Find the total cost. Also decide, without computing, whether the cost is greater than ₹18.4, and give one reason.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Strip points: 184 × 125 = 23000. Total decimal places: 1 + 1 = 2. Product = 230.00 = ₹230. The cost is greater than ₹18.4 because both factors are greater than 1, so the product must be greater than either factor.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the count-the-places multiplication rule; then use the both-greater-than-1 case from the sign-of-size table to justify the size of the product.

inclusivity.support: Let the student first estimate by rounding 18.4 to 18 and 12.5 to 13, multiplying to get 234, and then compute the exact answer for comparison.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find a different length (not 12.5 m) that would make the total cost exactly ₹230, explaining how they found it using division.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 12.2 p.73

items.prompt: A 17.5 kg sack of rice is distributed equally among 4 families. Using the place-value long-division method, find each family's share in kilograms.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 17.5 ÷ 4: divide 17 by 4 — quotient 4, remainder 1. Place decimal point in quotient. Regroup 1 one into 10 tenths; 10 tenths + 5 tenths = 15 tenths. 15 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 3. Regroup 3 tenths into 30 hundredths. 30 ÷ 4 = 7 remainder 2. Regroup 2 hundredths into 20 thousandths. 20 ÷ 4 = 5 remainder 0. Quotient = 4.375 kg.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply place-value long division, placing the decimal point in the quotient when ones are first regrouped into tenths, and continuing until the remainder is zero.

inclusivity.support: Let the student use the equivalent-fraction method first: 17.5/4 = 175/40, then simplify and scale to get 4375/1000 = 4.375, as a check before the long division.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to verify the answer by multiplying 4.375 × 4 and explain what the product confirms about the division.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.3 p.83
exercise.description: Find the quotient by converting the denominator into 1, 10, 100, or 1000 and verify by long division: (a) 18/5; (b) 415/4; (c) 1217/2; (d) 4827/8.

items.prompt: A tank holds 54.6 litres of water. It is filled using a can that holds 1.4 litres per scoop. How many full scoops are needed to fill the tank? Show your working by converting the divisor to a whole number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 54.6 ÷ 1.4: multiply both by 10 to get 546 ÷ 14. 546 ÷ 14 = 39 exactly. So 39 full scoops are needed.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply dividend and divisor by the same power of ten to make the divisor a whole number, then perform whole-number long division.

inclusivity.support: Let the student first estimate by rounding 1.4 to 1 and checking whether the quotient is close to 54.6, then carry out the exact method.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find the new answer if the can instead holds 1.05 litres per scoop, and explain which power of ten is needed this time.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 12.3 p.83

items.prompt: A school buys 6.48 kg of modelling clay and shares it equally among 1.2 kg portions for different classes. How many classes receive a full portion? Show your working by making the divisor a whole number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6.48 ÷ 1.2: multiply both by 10 to get 64.8 ÷ 12. 64.8 ÷ 12 = 5.4. So 5 classes receive a full 1.2 kg portion and 0.4 of a portion (0.48 kg) remains.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Scale the divisor to a whole number by multiplying dividend and divisor by 10, then divide; the whole-number part of the quotient is the number of full portions.

inclusivity.support: Let the student convert 1.2 to 12/10 and 6.48 to 648/100, then compute (648/100) ÷ (12/10) = (648/100) × (10/12) = 6480/1200 = 5.4 as a fraction route before the scaling method.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find how much clay would need to be added so that every class, including the partial one, receives exactly a full 1.2 kg portion.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 12.3 p.86

items.prompt: A 325 g jar of honey costs ₹97.5 and a 450 g jar of the same honey costs ₹135. Find the price per gram for each jar and decide which is the better buy.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Jar 1: 97.5 ÷ 325. Multiply both by 10: 975 ÷ 3250 — equivalently, 97.5/325 = 0.30 ₹/g. Jar 2: 135 ÷ 450 = 0.30 ₹/g. Both jars cost exactly ₹0.30 per gram, so neither is a better buy — they are identically priced per gram.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the cost by the weight in grams for each jar (making the divisor a whole number by appropriate scaling) and compare the per-gram prices.

inclusivity.support: Let the student compute how many grams each rupee buys (the reciprocal) as an alternative, using a simpler division, and compare.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find a third jar weight (between 325 g and 450 g) at which the price per gram would be ₹0.28, and explain how they set up the equation.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 12.4 p.93
exercise.description: A 210 g packet of peanut chikki costs ₹70.5 and a 110 g packet of potato chips costs ₹33.25; decide which is cheaper (per gram).

items.prompt: Using the fact that 756 ÷ 36 = 21, find 75.6 ÷ 3.6 and 7560 ÷ 3.6. Show how scaling the dividend and divisor by the same power of ten connects each new division to the original.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply dividend and divisor by the same power of ten to recover the known fact 756 ÷ 36 = 21, then scale the quotient accordingly.

inclusivity.support: Let the student write each division as a fraction and simplify step by step to see which scaling recovers 756/36.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find 0.756 ÷ 0.036 using the same approach, explain the result, and identify which entry in the Figure it Out Q8 table this matches.
